Review of the book "Iran and America: Sanctions, Wars, and the Policy of Mutual Containment" by Mohammad Fazeli

Yesterday, on the 27th of Mehr, I finally finished Part Four of the book "Iran and America: Sanctions, Wars, and the Policy of Mutual Containment" by Sasan Fayazmanesh, an Iranian economist living in America. The book was written in 2007 and translated into Persian in 1399, and it was published.

Part One
America and Iran: The Policy of Mutual Containment (The Years of Revolution and War)
https://castbox.fm/vb/986238431

Part Two
America and Iran: The Policy of Mutual Containment (Israel and the Clinton Era)
https://castbox.fm/vb/986238432

Part Three
America and Iran: The Policy of Mutual Containment (The George W. Bush Administration and the Nuclear File)
https://castbox.fm/vb/1005699834

Part Four
America and Iran: The Policy of Mutual Containment (Going to the Security Council)
https://castbox.fm/vb/1014998664

This book is not the only documented account, accompanied by detailed examination, of the Iran-America relationship from the moment of the 1357 revolution and the events that followed in the relations between Iran, America, and Israel; but it is a largely unheard, untold, and overlooked account of the consequences of this narrative. If you are interested in understanding the history of the America-Iran dispute, the role of Israel, and why the current situation exists, this book is an important work. The book was published by Nashr-e Negah-e Moaser with translation by Majid Khabir Sufian.

One of the important yet under-examined questions in Iran's contemporary history is why Iran, in the age of colonialism, despite its economic and military weakness and its proximity to two great imperial powers, managed to preserve its political independence and avoid becoming a formal colony. In the nineteenth century, before the discovery of oil, Iran—unlike India—did not possess vast, contiguous agricultural lands with a high capacity for producing commercial crops. Unlike China, it had no consumer market with a population in the hundreds of millions, and unlike certain other territories, known gold and silver mines were not the primary source of its economic appeal to colonial powers. Nor was Iran part of the Ottoman Empire, such that it would have been caught up in the partition of Ottoman territories among the European powers. Nevertheless, Iran held extraordinary geopolitical importance. Its geographic position—between Tsarist Russia and British-ruled India—had made the country one of the most important arenas of imperial rivalry. Under such circumstances, Iran's survival cannot be attributed merely to chance or to a lack of resources attractive to colonialists. The outcome of the war: Iran's hand is not empty
Having agency, or becoming Vietnam
In this conversation, Dr. Rahman Ghahremanpour reviews various theoretical approaches to the causes and roots of the war and explains the most important ones. Dividing the causes of war into two categories—structural and contingent—he also examines the mechanisms by which the war continues. Watch the conversation
https://youtu.be/2kNSgfijHjc
But the most important part of the conversation concerns his assessment of scenarios for the war's continuation. Although Ghahremanpour does not deny that some in America and Israel are pursuing the Iraq 2003 scenario, he believes the most likely outcome is something similar to what happened in the Balkan War and Serbia. Ghahremanpour lays out a map of Iran's capabilities that give the Iranian politician agency and allow for action in this crisis, showing which capabilities Iranians can rely on to get through this crisis at lower cost. For this reason, he believes Iran's hand is not empty.
